data.title: Who beat Huang Renxun to the punch?
data.description:
Capitol Hill is never short of investment gurus.

The most renowned among them is former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi, whose 38-year congressional career yielded a cumulative return of approximately 16,930%, exceeding the Dow Jones Industrial Average by seven times. This year, California Democratic Representative Roe Carnegie completed a trade that even Pelosi would envy.

On September 4th and October 7th, Carnegie's wife's affiliated trust sold Nvidia shares twice. Coincidentally, Nvidia's stock price had just hit a record high on October 6th. A little over a month later, the AI ​​bubble was ultimately burst by Xiaotou Literature, leading to Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO and a 35% plunge in Nvidia's stock price.

The Carnegie couple had also previously sold two shares near Nvidia's peak in May, only to buy them back in the third quarter, demonstrating considerable skill in swing trading. So far this year, Carnegie has disclosed 4,578 trades, outperforming the S&P 500 by 112.1% in the first four months alone.

However, as the person with the highest turnover rate on Capitol Hill, Carne actively pushed for a ban on members of Congress trading stocks. But this is not realistic. The average annual salary of a member of Congress is only $174,000, and there has been no salary increase in 17 years[1], not to mention that even the president himself is a trading expert. After Trump returned to the White House, he traded Nvidia 103 times, involving a total amount of $27 million to $97.5 million. In January 2025, Nvidia was hit by DeepSeek and plummeted. Just two days before Huang Renxun's first visit to the White House, Trump's account quietly bought $1 million to $5 million. The most recent operation occurred in August, when he bought $1.6 million of Nvidia and sold $1 million at the same time. As an ally of Huang Renxun, Nvidia has always been a major holding of Trump. In contrast, Carne is both a member of Congress where Nvidia is headquartered and the ranking Democrat on the Special Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and China, directly involved in discussions on chip export policies. Such precise timing of the sale inevitably raises questions about his unique background. Besides the Carners, top asset management giants such as the Soros family office, Blue Crown Capital, Bridgewater, Sixth Street, and Capital Group all reduced their holdings in Nvidia in the third quarter, with Renaissance Technologies almost completely selling off its entire stake. From Capitol Hill to Wall Street, a group of people most adept at dealing with information sold off their Nvidia shares one after another. What danger did they sense before Huang Renxun's departure? Ripples Those who have watched "Ming Dynasty 1566" know that the two most effective accusations for eliminating hostile forces are lust and collusion with Japanese pirates. Unexpectedly, centuries later, this combination of accusations has hit Huang Renxun. The first to target Huang Renxun's allegedly immoral private life was a short-selling firm called Culper Research. The two most talked-about financial articles in the world this year are Citrini Research's 3rd analyst's war diary in the Strait of Hormuz and Culper's cross-border tracking of Nvidia's China business. Two little-known small institutions have managed to revive non-fiction writing in the financial world. Culper was founded in 2019 and is located in an apartment in Brooklyn. The team consists of only four members: founder Lamarco, two analysts, and a Shiba Inu.[2] Culper's name comes from the Culper Ring, a spy network established by George Washington during the American Revolutionary War. In his view, short selling research and espionage have some similarities: collecting hard-to-obtain clues and piecing together scattered information into a complete map. Just like the "mosaic theory" believed by Citrini founder James Citrin, the real wealth is not in the public financial reports, but in many small, high-cost information fragments that may be ignored by mainstream institutions.

Christian Lamarco Daisy Korpics/WSJ, Bloomberg

In its short-selling report, Culper's core argument is that while Nvidia has ostensibly withdrawn from the Chinese market, a large number of GPUs may continue to serve Chinese customers through Southeast Asian intermediaries. China still contributes 20% of Nvidia's computing power revenue, and with export restrictions and domestic substitution in China, this will bring a huge financial blow to Nvidia.

Interestingly, Culper discovered a close relationship between Jensen Huang and Huang Le. Huang Le once boasted at a gathering that he could summon Jensen Huang, who indeed quickly appeared. An employee revealed that Huang Le is the behind-the-scenes boss of Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's largest chip buyers in Southeast Asia.

Culper even analyzed the video of the two leaving the noodle shop frame by frame, stopping at 3 minutes and 27 seconds: Huang Le saw the reporters outside, abruptly stopped, turned back to ask the woman in gray for her opinion, and continued forward after receiving a signal. On May 13, 2026, Lamarco, having spent a sleepless night, finished a bagel and a cigarette, and released this 40-page short-selling report, stating at the beginning that he held a short position in Nvidia. At this time, Huang Renxun was arriving in Beijing aboard Air Force One. The next day, Nvidia's stock price hit a record high. Six months earlier, few people paid attention to this short-selling report; Nvidia's stock price rose steadily, and Lamarco's hard-won report ultimately failed to gain traction. However, in the second quarter, the bullish forces on Nvidia weakened. Point72 reduced its holdings by 94.2%, and Third Point and Greenwoods Hong Kong almost completely liquidated their positions. In May, the Canners quietly sold two Nvidia shares, with the prodigy Leopold holding put options worth approximately $1.57 billion, foreshadowing his later margin call. It wasn't until October 29th, when the New York Times exposed the espionage allegations, that Huang Jen-hsun faced intense public scrutiny. This is where the blue-wing mouthpieces are more insidious than Culper; a sex scandal could only affect the Hangzhou prefect Gao Hanwen, but an espionage narrative could bring down the Zhejiang governor Hu Zongxian. With this two-pronged approach, even with strong fundamentals, Nvidia's stock price could be driven down. Since October 6th, short sellers have realized nearly $24 billion in paper profits in just 40 days. People began to relearn Culper's masterpiece; even Muddy Waters was inspired and focused on the personal relationships of another Nvidia executive. The ripples are now becoming clearer about the instigator of Huang Jen-hsun's departure. A serious internal division has emerged within the Republican Party. Hawks, represented by Rubio and Bessant, oppose selling chips to competitors, while populists, represented by Bannon and Hawley, oppose the rapid development of AI threatening MAGA's dominance. Together, they suppress the expansionists, represented by Trump and Lutnick. Coupled with the fanning of the flames by the severely declining pro-blue media, Jensen Huang has become a target for various political forces. However, in the third quarter, before Washington could even stage a House of Cards scenario, the aforementioned top Wall Street capital had already accelerated its exit. Domestic top capital showed the opposite trend. Gaoyi Capital International completely liquidated its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, and Greenwoods Hong Kong liquidated its holdings in the second quarter, but then bought them back in the third quarter, similar to Point72 and Third Point. Compared to TSMC, Greenwoods' Nvidia position was more of a exploratory one, with a small and very flexible position. Point72 operated similarly; even after buying back in the third quarter, it still reduced its common stock position by 77% compared to the first quarter. Third Point's Daniel Loeb's moves were even more flamboyant. Having just sold off his entire Nvidia stake in the second quarter, he bought back 1.5 million shares in the third quarter, making it his third-largest holding. Then, on November 3rd, he announced in an investor letter that he had significantly reduced his holdings in chips and data centers, expressing concern about whether the trillions of dollars in AI capital expenditure could recoup costs. In summary, Wall Street's bearish stance stems from three main concerns: Do customers still have the money to buy chips? Will the purchased chips have enough power to operate? Even if they do, will customers still necessarily buy Nvidia in the future? First, the cycle of revolving financing is quickly becoming unsustainable. Insurance companies were originally the main source of funding for chip financing, providing loans at interest rates of 5%-6.5%. However, as financing for tech giants like Microsoft and Nvidia reached the insurance company's single-customer concentration limit, borrowers were forced to seek higher-cost funding sources. Daniel Loeb's quarterly report indicated that the US credit market was entering a frenzy. High-yield bonds and leveraged loans for multiple data centers are yielding double-digit percentages; top-tier data center ABS priced below 5% in January now yield nearly 7%; credit default swap prices for Oracle, Meta, and Nvidia hit record highs in late October. With interest rates rising and returns on data center investments thinning, Nvidia is slowly transforming from a chip seller into a major financier providing financing to chip buyers. Then, AI computing power construction hit a power wall. Alan Waxman, who previously headed Goldman Sachs' largest proprietary investment division and now runs the $140 billion alternative asset management giant Sixth Street, recently estimated that approximately $200 billion worth of chips are sitting in warehouses, waiting for unbuilt data centers to be powered. Rising financing costs threaten Nvidia's orders, and power bottlenecks are slowing order fulfillment. But more critically, Nvidia's major customers are figuring out how to buy fewer chips from it. A recent JPMorgan report indicates that CUDA's moat is crumbling. According to their statistics, the computing power distribution of frontier labs after 2026 is as follows: Broadcom 23%, AMD 18%, Amazon Trainium 16%, Google TPU 14%, Cerebras 2%, and Nvidia only 28%. Michael Burry, who has been shorting Nvidia for a year, also noticed this change and recently shorted the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, bypassing the iShares Semiconductor ETF, which has a higher weighting of AMD and Broadcom. Recalling 2024, Peter Thiel made a discouraging remark at the All-In Summit: Nvidia is making so much money that everyone will try to replicate it in the chip industry. Two years later, Silicon Valley giants are fulfilling Thiel's prediction. After Huang Renxun left the company, a core question emerged: Is the departure of a legendary founder of a company a reason for Long Only Fund to sell? Duan Yongping neither shorted nor increased his investment. He believed that it would not have an impact on Nvidia's business in the short term. In a few years, it would depend on whether they could find a good CEO. Huang Renxun is a very hardworking person and has a great vision for the future of AI. It is difficult to find such a person. Matthew Witheiler, the investment manager of Wellington, the major shareholder of Nvidia, believes that Nvidia's product roadmap for the next two or three years has been determined. The CUDA ecosystem, R&D team and customer relationships will not disappear overnight with Huang Renxun's departure. No matter who takes the helm, Nvidia will still be the dominant supplier in the AI ​​computing power market. Wellington's bond fund manager even felt that changing CEOs may not be a bad thing. The successor's tolerance for risk may be lower than that of Huang Renxun[2]. In a sense, Jensen Huang is not only the CEO of Nvidia, but also the central bank governor of the AI ​​computing power market. While selling GPUs to customers, he also channeled funds to downstream computing power companies through equity investment, financing support, and procurement commitments. Under his impetus, the entire AI industry has experienced round after round of credit expansion. For a market accustomed to credit expansion, what will happen when a Volcker-style governor is suddenly appointed? Wall Street should know better than anyone else. References [1] Legislative Branch Appropriations: Frequently Asked Questions [2] The 31-Year-Old Trader Who Called Out Jensen Huang's 'China Problem'—and Shorted Nvidia,wsj [3] Nvidia turmoil marks the end of easy money for the AI ​​trade

data.title: Anthropic IPO Countdown: How Many Chinese Have Achieved Financial Freedom
data.description:
Article by Jedi, TOP Chinese Science and Technology Innovation Society

A "monstrous fortune" is about to be realized

On the evening of November 18th, Eastern Time, Anthropic set its offering price at $83 per share (valuing the company at nearly $1.5 trillion), exceeding the upper limit of the original $70 to $78 range; the offering size was subsequently expanded to 980 million shares, raising approximately $81.3 billion in public offering—the largest IPO in history in terms of fundraising amount. The previous week, the oversubscription rate on the subscription book was close to 7 times.

Tonight, Beijing Time, it will begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

A company with approximately 5,300 employees will have over 1,000 holding stock worth tens of millions of dollars. According to The Observer, Hill, a private equity market tracking platform, estimates that in a valuation scenario exceeding $1.5 trillion, the stock holdings of Anthropic's approximately 4,250 employees could be worth millions of dollars, with about 1,200 holding stock worth tens of millions of dollars and 50 early employees holding stock worth hundreds of millions of dollars. This estimate excludes the seven co-founders. SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's breakdown of the prospectus offers a more direct perspective: the net value of employee stock options and unvested RSUs totals approximately $216 billion, averaging about $41 million per person. Even more striking is that some of these individuals were not early hires. Business Insider, citing Levels.fyi's compensation sample in March of this year, reported that an engineer who joined Anthropic at the end of 2024 could have a vested equity valuation of $4 million to $5 million after a little over a year; another business operations head with two years of experience would have an equity valuation of approximately $9 million. They didn't found a company or invest capital as investors; instead, they participated in the growth of the company's value through equity attached to their jobs. Faced with such growth, which company you work for might have a greater impact on your wealth outcome than how much your next job will pay you. **Among this group, there are quite a few Chinese.** **Yuntao Bai participated in the early training method research at Anthropic; Yanda Chen trained Claude's programming and agent capabilities; Angela Jiang is in charge of the developer platform; and Cat Wu left before the IPO to join OpenAI.** **However, it's important to note that this is not a company without controversy in Chinese public opinion.** **In September 2025, Anthropic updated its terms of service, prohibiting companies whose "ownership structure is controlled by unlicensed jurisdictions such as China" from using its services, regardless of where these companies operate.** On the 19th of the same month, Yao Shunyu, one of the company's top researchers and a Chinese, issued a resignation letter, stating directly: "40% of the reason for leaving is my strong opposition to Anthropic's anti-China rhetoric, especially the statement that refers to China as a 'hostile country'."

In the following three months, the turnover rate of Chinese employees at Anthropic once exceeded 20%. Yuntao Bai and Cat Wu, who are on this list, later went to OpenAI.

Early Joining: Betting on an Unproven Future

Yuntao Bai's name appears at the very beginning of a key Anthropic paper. In 2022, the company published "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback," with Yuntao Bai as the first author. This work later became a highly recognizable part of Anthropic's technological roadmap. His academic background is theoretical physics.

After completing his PhD at Princeton and doing postdoctoral research at Caltech, he participated in the fine-tuning and alignment work at Anthropic, and later went to OpenAI. Jesse Mu, who graduated with a PhD from Stanford in 2023 and joined the Anthropic alignment team, followed the same path. He holds a bachelor's degree in Computer Science from Boston College, a master's degree from Cambridge, and a PhD from Stanford. He is one of the authors of *Sleeper Agents*, a study that demonstrates that models can retain implanted deceptive behavior even after secure training. Looking back today, participating in early research at a leading modeling company can easily be seen as a correct career choice. But in the very early stages, the only things you can judge are the team and the research direction. And staying was not an easy decision either. In the latter half of 2025, when the ban was issued, Yao Shunyu resigned, and Chinese researchers left en masse, this group chose to stay, and that choice has now become a paper fortune.

Mid-term entry: Catching up with the two fastest growth periods

Yanda Chen entered Anthropic in another phase

He completed his undergraduate degree in computer science at Columbia University in 2021 and received his PhD in the summer of 2024.

After joining Anthropic, he first worked in the Alignment team researching secure pre-training, mind chain interpretability, and AI control. Now he's moved to the Code RL team to train Claude's programming and agent capabilities, a core aspect of Claude's performance improvement.

Along with him in the same mid-term cohort were: Daliang Li, a Peking University physics graduate and Yale PhD, who previously worked in research engineering at Google and joined in 2024; Zhenze Fu, a Peking University mathematics and finance graduate, who previously worked in quantitative finance at Morgan Stanley and joined in 2024; Kaidi Cao, a Tsinghua University graduate and Stanford PhD, co-founder of Voyage AI, who joined in 2025 and is responsible for Claude's agent and tool usage training; and Zhipeng Jia, a University of Texas at Austin computer science PhD, who previously worked on AI systems research at Google and joined in June 2025.

Those who joined mid-term missed the initial low exercise price but benefited from the two years of fastest valuation growth.

The magnitude of the earnings depends on the size of the stock option grant, not just on the order of joining the company. The entry points are also broadening. Angela Jiang is responsible for the Claude Platform product; previously, she was responsible for the API platform at OpenAI and payment products at Stripe. Theodora Chu is responsible for the MCP (Model Context Protocol) product; after this protocol, which allows models to uniformly connect to external tools, was open-sourced, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI successively adopted it. Dickson Tsai participated in the engineering development of Claude Code. Barry Zhang and his colleagues wrote "Building Effective Agents," teaching enterprises to build agents starting with simple solutions. The people model companies need have expanded from "being able to build models" to "being able to turn models into products."

There's another group of people who aren't on the revenue chain, but who determine whether a product can be trusted: Jerry Wei led a team to build a security system for the production environment; Saffron Huang researched the social impact of models; Rowan Wang, Belinda Zou Li, and Newton Cheng respectively worked on alignment, interpretability, and the cutting-edge red team.

This is especially meaningful for Chinese people with experience in large companies: their previously accumulated platform, engineering, and product experience has the opportunity to be revalued in a faster-growing company. Skills don't have to be completely rebuilt; the places where they are used can change.

The Eve of the IPO: Those Who Left and Those Who Arrived

Cat Wu Didn't Get to Hear the Bell Ring

She graduated from Princeton's Computer Science department and started her career as an early product engineer at Scale AI. Later, she worked as an investor at Index Ventures—product, growth, capital—she's been at every link in this chain.

After joining Anthropic, she became the product lead for Claude Code, turning an internal tool into one of the company's fastest-growing products. At the developer conference this May, she was one of the most talked-about speakers. In early November, she announced her move to OpenAI to manage core products. Leaving before an IPO can easily be interpreted as giving up a significant sum of money. However, employee benefits don't only materialize on the day of the IPO; the experience of creating a hit product is itself something a new company is willing to pay. Sihao Huang, on the other hand, joined Anthropic three months before the IPO and immediately became the highest-ranking Chinese employee known to hold. His resume doesn't resemble that of a model researcher. Born in Guangzhou, raised in Singapore, and moved to the United States at age 14; while in high school, he founded the rocket company Aphelion Orbitals in New York, serving as CEO; he then entered MIT, earning double degrees in physics and electrical engineering, with a minor in political science; after graduating with his bachelor's degree, he entered Tsinghua University as a Schwarzman Scholar, and later went to Oxford as a Marshall Scholar; afterwards, he left his doctoral program to enter the government, serving as a senior policy advisor on AI and emerging technologies in the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. This September, he joined Anthropic as Head of Frontier Computing Strategy, partnering with co-founder and Chief Computing Officer Tom Brown. Even later is Bingjie Tang. She joins in November 2026, holding a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Southern California, and previously worked on dexterity maneuvers on Tesla's Optimus team. For such latecomers, the early valuation growth is no longer an opportunity to participate. The opportunity lies in something else: what capabilities does the company need in the next stage, and what are they willing to sacrifice for it?

Sharing the rewards of entrepreneurship without starting a business

Do top-tier technical talents necessarily have to start their own companies to reap the rewards of a life-changing transformation?

Anthropic's answer is no: continue doing research, writing code, and developing products, with the company organizing capital, computing power, and customers, and then sharing growth through equity. Whether one is suitable to be a founder is not the same as whether one can share the rewards of entrepreneurship. But rewards are never determined solely by ability; which company one joins, what terms one accepts, and when one sells all rewrite the outcome; those equity stakes that ultimately go to zero won't be reported.

For this group of Chinese, what's truly worth observing is the next step. The practical meaning of financial freedom is that it allows people to take on career risks they wouldn't otherwise dare to take. Anthropic needs to consider how to retain them; and for the first time, they are able to answer that question: if they didn't have to stay for money, what else would they want to do?

data.title: MEV Acquittal: Why BlackRock Values ​​This On-Chain Trial
data.description:
Written by: Daii

A $25 million on-chain comeback ultimately stalled on an age-old legal question: Who made what promise to whom? Understanding this is crucial to discerning what the acquittal protected and which on-chain actions it didn't excuse.

Imagine you're buying something at a small shop. Someone sees your order first, buys the item, and then sells it to you at a slightly higher price. This early birder makes money daily by observing other people's orders. One day, he sees a familiar large order, buys it as usual, only to find that the order didn't go through as expected; the item remains in his hands, but the other party has taken the real money. This controversy on Ethereum in 2023 has such a dramatic twist. But the court's question wasn't who was more likable, but whether that order, that signature, made a legally valid false promise.

(Court ruling, pp. 11-16, 34-39)

On November 16, a U.S. federal judge acquitted brothers Anton and James Peraire-Bueno. BlackRock had previously included their criminal case in the prospectus of its Ethereum staking fund: if MEV is ultimately found illegal, the fund's staking business may be disrupted. Why did a dispute between on-chain transaction bots enter the risk disclosure of a Wall Street fund? The answer lies in an Ethereum block proposal: the network currently enters a new time slot every 12 seconds, but not every time slot produces a block. (Court ruling, pp. 1, 4-5; BlackRock Ethereum Staking Fund Prospectus, "MEV" Risk Section; Ethereum Official Block Proposal Explanation)

First, understand the person who makes money by "queuing"

Ethereum transactions are not mechanically recorded according to the order in which you click the button.

Transactions must first enter the processing queue before being added to a block; the order in which transactions are processed affects prices on decentralized exchanges. MEV, or "Maximum Extractable Value," refers to the additional value participants gain by incorporating, excluding, and ordering transactions. It takes various forms, including arbitrage and liquidation, and not all MEVs constitute an attack; one of the most controversial forms is the "sandwich attack": a bot sees your buy order, buys at the front to drive up the price, causing your transaction to be executed at a lower price, and then sells at the back to profit. Ordinary traders bear higher transaction costs. (Court ruling, pp. 4-5, 11-12; Ethereum Foundation MEV explanation) Nowadays, professional bots typically deliver a "buy-sandwich target transaction-sell" transaction combination to the block builder, which then relays it via MEV-Boost to the validator responsible for proposing the block. Think of it as a sealed performance program: the validator sees the program cover (the block header), signs it, and then the relay reveals the full content. This design was intended to encourage bidders to compete, while preventing validators from copying others' ordering schemes before payment or commitment. The bot assumed that as long as the entire set of transactions entered the same block in the predetermined order, it would immediately sell the coins it bought, avoiding the risk of long-term holding. (Court judgment, pp. 7-12, Flashbots MEV-Boost document)

The key distinction here is that the three professional traders referred to as "victim traders" in this case operated bots that sought sandwich opportunities; their losses do not mean that the ordinary users they previously sandwiched did not incur costs. (Court judgment, pp. 11-13)

How the brothers lured the sandwiching bot into their own trap

Court records show that the brothers began studying the behavior of the target bots in late 2022, establishing 16 validators and repeatedly testing what kind of transactions would attract them.

On April 2, 2023, when it was the validators' turn to propose a block, they sent eight "bait transactions" into the public queue. The bots treated these transactions as easy targets, submitting combinations of buy orders, bait transactions, and sell orders. The initial indictment described the entire process as acquiring approximately $25 million in about 12 seconds; this is the prosecution's figure and narrative, not a separate civil accounting of each loss by the judge. (Court ruling, pp. 12–15; U.S. Department of Justice indictment, pp. 8–11) Let's first look at what the relay holds. The block builder submits a complete list containing transactions that have not yet been published; validators initially only see the block header without transaction content, and only after signing it can they obtain the list. The block header contains two "fingerprints" that must be correct: the parent block root indicates which old block the new block follows, and the state root reflects the current on-chain state. If either one is incorrect, the entire block cannot be accepted by Ethereum. A signature only proves who signed the block header, not that the block header was filled in correctly. If the relay submits the list before confirming the block's validity, validators have the opportunity to view other people's transactions and then rewrite their own blocks. (Court judgment, pp. 7-10, Flashbots incident review) The vulnerability lies precisely in this crucial point. The open-source program used by the Ultrasound relay in the case verified that the signature came from the validator who was supposed to propose the block and checked the existence of fields, but it did not verify whether the values ​​of the parent block root and state root were correct. Even if it was rejected by the Ethereum node after attempting to publish the block, the program would still deliver the complete transaction content to the validator. The Flashbots incident review attributes this to a relay implementation vulnerability; public information does not explain why the developers initially omitted the validity check, and the reason cannot be arbitrarily stated as "for speed" or "intentionally allowing it." (Court judgment, pp. 8-10, 14-16, 38-39; Flashbots incident review)

The brothers filled in 0 for the two fields that should have been specific fingerprints, and then signed them with their real keys. The signature verification passed because the signature did correspond to this "zero-filled block header"; however, this block header described an invalid block, which the real Ethereum nodes would not accept. The relay, however, handed over the sealed transaction list first. The first purpose of filling in zeros is to obtain private content with a valid signature, while preventing the original block from being added to the chain. There was no impersonation of someone else's private key here; the so-called "fake signature" refers to signing a block header with incorrect content. (Court judgment, pp. 14-16, 36-39; Flashbots incident review)

The second purpose is to eliminate competition. The original block was rejected, so it could not compete for the same time slot as the valid block subsequently submitted by the brothers.

They had already seen the bot's buying and selling arrangements, so they reserved the bot's first buy and swapped it for their own sell transaction, preventing the bot's final sell from completing as planned. The brothers' validators were penalized 1 ETH for proposing two blocks in the same time slot; the court-recorded losses for the traders were approximately $25 million. Flashbots subsequently modified its relay program: if the original block failed to be published, the transaction content would not be delivered to the validators. (Court judgment, pp. 15-17, Flashbots incident review and fix, Flashbots fix code)

A striking example from the trial: a bot operator said that on one occasion, his bot was willing to exchange approximately $2.3 million worth of USDC for SHIB at the time, which was only about $8.25, because the algorithm anticipated selling it back at a more favorable price immediately afterward. This was not a SHIB investment that an ordinary person would be willing to hold long-term, but an instantaneous transaction based on the premise that "the following two steps would be executed completely."

... This example illustrates that once a portfolio trade is broken up, what initially appears to be a small price difference can multiply into a huge exposure. (Court ruling, page 12) In May 2024, U.S. prosecutors indicted the brothers on charges of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, arguing that the bait, invalid block headers, and subsequent transfer of funds constituted a scam. The nearly four-week trial ended in 2025 with a jury unable to reach a unanimous verdict. On November 16, 2026, after reviewing the trial evidence, the judge granted a motion for acquittal and closed the case; this verdict was based on insufficient evidence, not a jury vote finding the entire strategy legitimate. (US Department of Justice 2024 Indictment and Court Judgment, pp. 1, 45-46) The judge didn't ask "How much is the loss?" but rather "Where is the lie?" The prosecution presented two core paths of "lying." First, the bait transaction appeared to the bot as a promise to be sandwiched and included in the final block as planned. The judge rejected this: a transaction appearing in the public queue only expresses "I want to make this transaction," without promising to be sandwiched or guaranteeing that any combination will be on-chain. The price difference the bot hopes to earn does not automatically become a contractual obligation of the bait party. Especially in an open network without uniform usage terms, the expectations of market participants cannot be written as a guarantee already made by the opponent. (Court Judgment, pp. 28-35) Second, the prosecution argued that signing the block header is equivalent to promising to publish the complete block as is. The judge still refused to accept that the signature, within the existing mechanism, identified the validator and made them potentially punishable for misconduct; it did not guarantee the block's validity or its inclusion on the blockchain. More critically, the relay failed to check the two zero-filled fields; since the recipient's release decision did not depend on the authenticity of the fields, the prosecution struggled to prove these erroneous fields constituted a "material misrepresentation" that led the other party to hand over the transaction details. The vulnerability was indeed exploited, and $25 million was indeed involved in the dispute, but wire fraud still requires proof of its specific legal elements. (Court ruling, pp. 36-40) The prosecution also attempted to link a series of covert actions to demonstrate that the entire scheme was a fraud. The judge acknowledged that the transaction strategy might be offensive, but stated that concealing the strategy, exploiting software flaws, and subsequent complex transfers could not replace the material misrepresentation required for wire fraud. The money laundering conspiracy charge in this case was predicated on proceeds from wire fraud; if the former failed, the latter also collapsed. The judgment clearly states its boundaries at the outset: it does not determine whether the conduct was morally sound, nor does it address other unprosecuted charges or civil disputes. (Court Judgment, pp. 1, 40-46) The value of this acquittal lies primarily in drawing a verifiable line in criminal law: the existence of substantial losses from on-chain actions cannot preclude proof of "to whom the defendant made what false statements, and whether the other party changed their behavior accordingly." It also reminds protocol designers that economic penalties, coding practices, and legal commitments are three distinct things. If a critical step must be credible, the software should verify it; if an action must be contractually binding, terms that can be proven to be accepted should be written. An acquittal does not equate to "any MEV being legal," but rather that the prosecution's arguments and the evidence presented did not cross the threshold for criminal conviction. (Court judgment, pp. 28-46)

BlackRock is concerned that the returns also go through the same "ordering pipeline"

BlackRock's iShares Staked Ethereum Trust ETF does not hand over the fund's assets to these two companies. It allows service providers to use the fund's ETH for validation in order to obtain protocol rewards, transaction tips, and potential MEV returns. The prospectus states that staking service providers will include MEV in their revenue streams; if MEV is found to violate applicable laws, the fund's staking program may be interrupted, and the value of fund units may be affected. The prospectus also anticipates staking approximately 70%–95% of ETH under normal circumstances and discloses that sponsors and service chains collectively receive 18% of the gross staking returns, with the remainder remaining in the fund. The returns do not appear out of thin air: block ordering has a price, and the fund is participating in sharing this price.

(BlackRock Ethereum Staking Fund March 2026 Prospectus, "MEV", Staking Arrangements and Profit Distribution Section)

But we cannot confuse the concepts here. BlackRock's documents refer to the MEV-related rewards received by validators, not that the fund is directly operating sandwich bots, much less that it participated in the transactions exploiting the relay vulnerability in this case. MEV can come from different transaction arrangements; within the same profit pipeline, there may be ranking revenue from open auctions, or there may be squeeze revenue that passes on slippage to ordinary users. The court did not categorize them one by one, nor did it issue a "legal license" to the entire industry. For the fund, this acquittal reduces the threat of one of the broadest criminal interpretations, but it does not eliminate the legal risks related to regulation, contracts, reputation, and specific strategies. (BlackRock Prospectus, "MEV" Risk Section, Court Judgment, pp. 1, 45-46)

Another move by BlackRock is particularly intriguing: its staking agreement requires Coinbase to establish legally binding arrangements with validators and requires validators to commit to setting up controls such as anti-money laundering, sanctioned address screening, and regular testing; if a validator defaults, the fund can demand that Coinbase pursue legal action. This contrasts sharply with the case in which the prosecution failed to prove that the validators involved accepted a specific commitment to "post as signed," while the fund diligently incorporated key obligations into the contract within its own business chain. Contracts cannot guarantee absolute security; the prospectus explicitly states that if Coinbase and validators fail to fulfill their obligations, the costs of recovery and staking losses may still be borne by the fund and holders.

(BlackRock prospectus, "Staking Addendum" and "Approved Validator Schedule" terms)

After being acquitted, the real question to ask is who bears the ranking costs

This case provides readers with a more practical framework for judgment. When seeing "staking rewards," first ask whether the revenue is issued by the protocol, a priority fee voluntarily paid by traders, or a contribution from others bearing worse transaction prices; then ask how the rewards are distributed among the fund, custodian, and node operators; finally ask whether, if the ranking party violates its promises, it will be held accountable through on-chain penalties, software verification, or enforceable contracts. BlackRock's documents at least provide verifiable text about MEV rewards, the 18% fee allocation, and service provider obligations, but this is still insufficient to tell investors which trading strategy each MEV comes from. (BlackRock Prospectus, "MEV", Revenue Distribution and Staking Service Terms)

For ordinary on-chain traders, the most direct lesson is not to learn the brothers' methods. Before trading, check the slippage cap, price impact, and execution path, and use transaction protections that reduce exposure to the public pending queue when necessary; however, "private sending" still relies on the service provider's confidentiality and execution commitments and cannot be considered a zero-risk insurance. For protocols and institutions, it is more crucial to verify the complete data bound to the signature, clarify the obligations of block builders and validators, and record who accepted which rules. The market may ultimately choose to strengthen the code, fill the gaps with contracts, or have regulators define the boundaries; this ruling only tells us that criminal law cannot replace all the missing designs in one step.

... (Court judgment, pages 7-12, 36-46; Ethereum Foundation MEV description; BlackRock prospectus staking service terms) This is why BlackRock takes this case seriously, and why the acquittal is still worth reading carefully by all on-chain participants: what appears to be a mere $25 million dispute between bots has actually pushed the "transaction ordering right" from technical details to the legal and investor accounts. The court did not offer a moral pardon for MEV, but rather a proof question: loss does not equate to fraud; profit does not equate to no cost. The next step that truly determines the industry's direction is whether the source of profit, technical verification, and attribution of responsibility can be clearly stated. (Court judgment, pages 1, 36-46; BlackRock prospectus MEV risk and staking agreement)

data.title: Netflix's new series "Altruists" turns the FTX case into a love story.
data.description:
Author: Ben Weiss Source: Bloomberg Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

Julia Garner (left) as Caroline Ellison, Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried. Image source: Netflix © 2026

One ​​of the most sensational subplots in the entire FTX scandal—crypto mogul Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) stealing $8 billion from clients—was his affair with his deputy, Caroline Ellison. The two had a relationship early in their careers, and numerous private communications were used as evidence in court.

This relationship wasn't the only focus of the case (I covered this case in 2023); besides Ellison, other key witnesses testified against Bankman Fried. However, in Netflix's new series *The Altruists*, this entanglement has been thrust into the spotlight with its dramatic reimagining of the scandal. The eight-episode series condenses a complex financial crime story into a glamorous love story. And this rewriting—intentional or not—seems to absolve Bankman Fried of responsibility, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud. The series, which premiered on November 19th, is the latest in a string of tech-themed Hollywood productions. October's releases include Aaron Sorkin's *The Social Reckoning*, telling the story of a Facebook whistleblower; Alex Gibney's four-hour documentary *Musk*, a critical look at the tech giant; and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's genre-blending *You Can See Everything*, telling the story of Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the blood-testing startup Theranos, who was sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. Amid this wave of film and television releases, Netflix last month released a trailer for *Altruists*, packaging one of the biggest frauds in financial history as a Bonnie and Clyde-esque tale of a desperate love affair. “The collapse of FTX ruined many lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story,” wrote Constance Waing, former COO of the FTX cryptocurrency exchange.

The narrative in the show seems to absolve Bankman-Fried of responsibility for the fraud. Image credit: Netflix © 2026

I was initially skeptical of this narrative framework as well. I've been covering the crypto industry for years; during Bankman-Fried's trial, I would get up early to secure a seat in court and cover the proceedings. After reviewing the evidence and listening to hours of testimony, it seemed to me that the collapse of FTX wasn't a tragic love story, but rather a parable about how dangerous it is to make money too fast and too much.

"The Altruist" is written by Graham Moore, who won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay in 2015 for "The Imitation Game," a biopic about mathematician Alan Turing. Moore co-wrote the series with writers Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, who later wrote a series of in-depth investigative reports for *New York Magazine* about FTX and Bankman-Fried after the FTX collapse. Moore told me he did a lot of research himself, carefully reading court records, text messages, and other documents. "In particular, I was able to build my own sources inside and around FTX," he said, but declined to reveal who he interviewed specifically because he wanted to "keep the process intact."

The show's title comes from what Bankman-Fried calls his driving philosophy: effective altruism, a philanthropic doctrine that encourages believers to think quantitatively about how to maximize their impact on the world. Many effective altruists hold high-paying jobs and donate their earnings to charity. In the show, Bankman-Fried, played by Anthony Boyle (of *The Guinness Family* fame), does just that. After graduating from MIT, this mathematical genius works at the prestigious trading firm Jane Street. There, he meets his sweetheart, Ellison, played by Julia Garner (of *Weapons* and *Ozark* fame), and the two fall in love at first sight while solving math problems. Bankman-Fried conducts a training session where she bets on whether she can solve a series of brain teasers, and the two nervously exchange knowing smiles. Ellison shoved all his chips forward: “Going all in every time is the mathematically optimal strategy.” — This statement foreshadowed later events.

The relationship between Bankman Fried and Ellison is central to *The Altruist*. Image credit: Ricardo Hubbs/Netflix © 2026

Ellison and Bankman Fried began an on-again, off-again relationship, with the series following Fried's career trajectory. He left Jane Street to found the crypto hedge fund Alameda Research, recruiting Ellison and eventually appointing her as co-CEO. He then founded FTX, building a rapidly growing crypto exchange capable of competing with the largest companies in the market.

In 2022, Bankman-Fried's empire collapsed abruptly after a customer run exposed an $8 billion hole in its balance sheet. Facing the threat of prosecution, Ellison turned his attention to Bankman-Fried and cooperated with the US government. *The Altruist* attempts to simplify the jargon-laden and complex world of crypto—and to some extent succeeds. At the heart of the company's crimes is theft: customers' money isn't where it's supposed to be, and when customers want to withdraw, FTX doesn't have enough to pay them back. It's that straightforward. However, some scenes expose blind spots for the actors and writers. Ryan Salame, an FTX employee who had previously been imprisoned for campaign finance fraud, mispronounced the token code for Ethereum (the world's second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization) in the show. (That sound is a long "e".) Elsewhere, Ellison says that in the "Prisoner's Dilemma" (a game theory situation where participants can choose to cooperate with law enforcement or remain silent), the "mathematically optimal" choice is not to report. In fact, for a single game, the mathematically optimal solution is precisely to report. (The expected sentence for a whistleblower is always shorter than for someone who remains silent.) Moore artistically embellished the material. In a key scene, Ellison tells FTX employees that Alameda Research has been misappropriating customer funds from the exchange. However, according to court records, she actually said this to Alameda employees, not to employees of the cryptocurrency exchange. There are many similar discrepancies; for example, *The Altruist* portrays FTX CTO Gary Wang as an outspoken, foul-mouthed programmer, while court records show that Gary Wang was actually a taciturn coder. The TV series *Altruism* portrays Changpeng Zhao, co-founder of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an early investor in FTX, as the show's main antagonist. Played by Terry Chen (of *House of Cards* fame), Zhao sells his shares after pressuring Bankman Fried to leak non-public information about upcoming FTX transactions to Alameda Research for personal gain. In the show, Zhao implies that Bankman Fried could use this information for insider trading. This practice, known as "front-running," is illegal in most jurisdictions. While there is no evidence that Zhao pressured Bankman Fried to do so, the Binance co-founder did indeed sell his shares back to him in reality. The show deviates even further from the mainstream narrative by portraying Ellison as a partner almost equal to Bankman Fried, who conspired to embezzle client funds from FTX. "It's like the two of them were caught in some kind of insane sexual frenzy, constantly pushing each other to more extremes," says Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther, star of *Alien: Earth*), former co-CEO of Alameda Research, on his yacht, "Soak My Deck." (This last part is unfortunately true. Trabucco was later forced to surrender the yacht during FTX's bankruptcy proceedings.) The show portrays Ellison as a partner almost equal to Bankman Fried. Image source: Netflix © 2026

In a scene near the end of the series, a table shows FTX's major shareholders, including Ellison, who is plotting a coup to overthrow Bankman-Fried. But according to court records, in reality, Bankman-Fried, Gary Wong, and FTX's engineering chief Nishad Singh all held far more shares than Ellison. Former FTX executive Win told me that the usual "ultimate decision-maker" was Bankman-Fried, not Ellison. Jay Morakis, founder and CEO of the PR firm M Group, who worked closely with FTX and Bankman-Fried for nearly two years before the collapse, put it similarly: "He was everything."

Changpeng Zhao hasn't watched the show yet, but his expectations are low. "It won't accurately reflect what happened," he told me.

“I think Sam is a very smart guy. He was just too aggressive, too eager to succeed.” However, the show's writers seem to sympathize with Bankman Fried's account of why FTX ultimately collapsed. According to prosecutors, the FTX CEO conspired with Ellison and a small group of colleagues to take customer funds and invest them in a hodgepodge of investments, political donations, sponsorships, and real estate. These expenditures created an $8 billion funding gap for FTX. But Bankman Fried's lawyers have consistently argued that the money was there—just sitting in “illiquid” assets that could eventually be sold. Most notably, this was Bankman Fried's $500 million stake in Anthropic PBC. In the final episode of *Altruists*, Bankman Fried frantically—and futilely—attempted to sell his shares in the AI ​​company. Just before the end credits rolled, a title card told the audience how much his Anthropic investment was now worth—$100 billion. (Based on analysis of FTX bankruptcy filings and Anthropic IPO prices, the actual value of this investment could be as high as approximately $37 billion.) The presiding judge in the Bankman-Fried case ultimately rejected this argument. “It’s like saying, if I break into the Federal Reserve Bank, take a million dollars, buy it all in Powerball, and happen to win, that’s fine,” he said in court. Altruism is a work of fiction. Moore said he set a rule: if there is documentary evidence of a moment, that moment will not be included in the show. He wanted the show to have an intimacy, allowing viewers to glimpse the inner world of Bankman-Fried and Ellison in an unprecedented way. “What were Sam and Caroline whispering to each other in the dim light of night, pillow to pillow?” Moore wondered. A few days before I started watching the pilot episode of *Altruism*, I went to see *You Can See Everything* in theaters. The film stars actress Amanda Seyfried, who previously played Holmes in a Hulu series about Theranos. In the film, Holmes complains about Seyfried's inaccurate portrayal, and Seyfried gets angry. "This isn't a lie," she says, "this damn television." No dramatic adaptation can be completely realistic, but *Altruism* offers another interpretation of the case—although questions remain about the fraudsters' true motives, and the case has been appealed to the Supreme Court, it is essentially legally settled. I'm not sure if *Altruism* is a lie, but it certainly is television.

data.title: CZ missed out on a multi-billion dollar stake in Anthropic by refusing to pay $1 to FTX.
data.description:
CZ didn't reject a bankrupt exchange; he rejected a ticket to a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

—— Written on the Night of Anthropic's Bell Ringing

—— The $1 acquisition option back then is now Anthropic equity

Anthropic rang the bell on Nasdaq tonight, ticker symbol ANT, with a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion, setting a new global IPO fundraising record.

The moment the celebratory champagne popped, those who should have been watching the screen most closely weren't from Silicon Valley, but from the crypto community—especially Changpeng Zhao.

Because just three years ago, that company, which was about to create seven founders with net worths of tens of billions, was only one unsigned contract away from being listed on Binance's books.

Buy a trillion-dollar empire for $1

— FTX: The collapse only took a few days

In November 2022, FTX was bleeding hundreds of millions of dollars per hour.

SBF dialed CZ's number, speaking casually, "like ordering a Bologna sandwich"—opening with a request for billions of dollars in bailout.

— SBF: The Protagonist of That Phone Call

According to Blockworks at the time, citing sources, the initial acquisition price discussed by both parties was a symbolic $1. The price was taking over FTX's multi-billion dollar financial hole.

Binance quickly signed a non-binding letter of intent (LOI) for acquisition, and then withdrew even faster.

— Cover of CZ's memoir "Binance Life"

"I had no interest in owning FTX, nor was I particularly interested in helping SBF. Signing the letter of intent was just a formality, to let the team see the data first."

CZ later stated this very frankly in his memoir "Freedom of Money," clearing himself of any involvement.

What he rejected wasn't just FTX

Interestingly, hidden within FTX's asset portfolio was a nuclear bomb that no one could see at the time.

— That AI lab that couldn't even name Claude back then is now called Anthropic

In 2021, SBF, through Alameda, invested $500 million in Anthropic, an AI lab that couldn't even name Claude and was virtually unknown, acquiring approximately 13.56% of its initial equity. After dilution from subsequent rounds of financing, it still retained approximately 7.84% by 2024.

Roughly calculated based on a $1.5 trillion valuation: $1.5 trillion × 7.84% ≈ $117.6 billion

One hundred billion US dollars.

In other words, if CZ had just gritted his teeth and taken on that "$1 acquisition" back then, and also absorbed FTX's financial hole, the Binance Group might have an AI equity stake today that is larger than the GDP of most countries.

Two algorithms, two orders of magnitude

ScopeValuation
Undiluted percentage × Tonight's valuation (rough calculation)≈ $117.6 billion
Recalculated based on actual number of shares sold and IPO price rangeApproximately $31-35 billion

This is a "counterfactual deduction": it doesn't account for subsequent dilution, transaction structure, or ownership disputes under bankruptcy law. But even $35 billion would be enough to fill the $8 billion funding gap from back then four times over with some surplus.

SBF sold off its gold mine for pennies

— Anthropic's valuation soared (the image is from a previous report when it was valued at $1.4 trillion)

The irony continued. In 2024, the FTX bankruptcy consortium sold off its Anthropic shares in two batches: $884 million in March and $452 million in June, recovering a total of approximately $1.336 billion, at an average price of $30 per share.

$500 million｜Invested in 2021

$1.3 billion｜Recovered by liquidation in 2024

$500 million went in, $1.3 billion came out, a profit of more than double on paper—in the context of bankruptcy liquidation, this is already a "graceful exit."

But looking back today: if those shares had been held until tonight, their value would have increased more than twentyfold. The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund ATIC, which took over, invested $500 million back then and now holds approximately $13.8 billion; Jane Street's $100 million has become $2.7 billion.

And SBF himself, in prison, could only smile bitterly at the New York Times camera. He once issued a 30-page statement titled "FTX: Where Did the Money Go?"—Anthropic was the first piece of evidence he listed.

If CZ really got it, would he still invest in Kimi?

Another rumor circulated in the market this year: YZi Labs invested in Kimi, the Dark Side of the Moon.

— YZi Labs' AI Investment Reach

He Yi's response was very nuanced—"It's an investment in a Chinese-owned AI company," neither confirming nor denying.

This is actually a rather subtle footnote. If Binance had really acquired Anthropic back then, CZ would already hold one of the world's top large-scale model companies, and wouldn't have needed to rush to find a place in the Chinese large-scale model market midway through the AI ​​wave.

He later traveled the world looking at AI projects, investing in robotics, agents, and education—more like trying to catch up on a missed opportunity years ago.

Was it risk aversion, or a missed opportunity?

Back to the unavoidable question: Was abandoning the acquisition of FTX a precise risk avoidance strategy, or the most expensive abandonment in the AI ​​era?

From a transaction logic perspective, CZ was right.

FTX's financial problems, compliance risks, regulatory hostility, and user runs—any one of these would have been enough to severely damage Binance. Taking over wasn't a heroic rescue; it was jumping into a fire pit.

But in the end, he avoided the fire pit, and also avoided the gold buried beneath it.

The market never rewards "correct rejections," only "the final accounting."

On the night Anthropic rang its bell, CZ probably also saw this news.

Hidden within the ruins he had initially refused to take over was a multi-billion dollar AI bet that could have belonged to Binance.

data.title: From Digital Wallets to US Futures Exchanges: Backpack's Four Years
data.description:
Author: insights4vc Source: insights4vc (Substack) Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

When FTX collapsed in November 2022, the Backpack team had $14.5 million trapped in the exchange, approximately 88% of its operating capital. Four years later, this company, which started as a digital wallet, has received approval in the United States to operate a futures exchange, clear trades, and serve clients through its own brokerage business.

The most intuitive way to understand what Backpack is building is to follow the path of Micron stock. In eligible markets, clients can buy this stock through Backpack, transfer the digital certificate representing it to their own wallet, and then use this certificate as collateral for loans.

Clients continue to have exposure to Micron stock while borrowing from lenders outside of the brokerage business. On November 18th, Backpack's official account tweeted that following obtaining exchange and clearinghouse licenses this Monday, the company has received NFA approval to operate as a Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), becoming the first CFTC-regulated exchange to introduce leveraged perpetual contracts with unified global liquidity to the United States. Investors are already trading these tokens. In the third quarter of 2026, Backpack's securities accounted for 44% of the tokenized stock trading volume on the Solana decentralized exchange. These trades occurred in other venues, and fees were collected by those venues. As Backpack prepares to open its US futures exchange, the question becomes: what can transfer these orders, and the client balances behind those orders, into its own ledger?

Before the Exchange

Backpack started in 2022, betting on how people would use Solana applications. Armani Ferrante had previously developed the Solana development framework Anchor and also participated in Serum's on-chain order book. He and Tristan Yver developed a wallet that allows applications to run within executable NFTs (xNFTs): developers put an application into a customer's wallet, and the customer opens it directly from there. In September 2022, the team behind the wallet, Coral, announced the completion of a $20 million strategic round, co-led by FTX Ventures and Jump Crypto, with participation from Multicoin Capital, Anagram, K5 Global, and Frictionless.

Backpack Milestones

Two months later, FTX went bankrupt. According to Backpack itself, $14.5 million of its operating funds, equivalent to 88% of its reserves, were tied up in FTX. The team subsequently launched Mad Lads in April 2023 and a beta version on an exchange in November of the same year. This NFT series gave the founders a directly reachable audience when the exchange opened. In March 2024, TechCrunch reported that 560,000 users had completed identity verification. Backpack did not specify how many of these people later actually deposited funds and continued trading.

The exchange's public contract beta version went live in January 2025. By September, the group was offering regulated derivatives in Europe. In January 2026, private testing of grid trading and prediction market products followed; BP tokens were issued in March; and the securities business was launched in June. Along the way, the additions to the team also made the changes in the business visible: CTO Thomas Linton, Chief Compliance Officer Can Sun who previously served as General Counsel of FTX International, became the CTO. Former CFTC Commissioner and Acting Chairman Mark Wetjen became President of Backpack US, and former SEC Commissioner Michael Piwowar joined its US Board of Directors.

Who funded Backpack and what did they acquire?

The two funding rounds usually associated with Backpack actually invested in different things. Coral's 2022 investors were betting on an app wallet; Jump's Kanav Kariya was talking about how developers could combine apps, while FTX's Ramnik Arora saw an opportunity in an app store. By February 2024, investors were able to price a fully operational exchange. Placeholder led the first tranche of a $17 million Series A funding round for companies in the Backpack ecosystem, valuing the company at a total of $120 million. The announcement listed investors including Hashed, Robot Ventures, Amber Group, Wintermute Ventures, Selini Capital, and Delphi Digital, as well as founders from Solana, Tensor, Jito, Zeta, Marginfi, Drift, Monad, and Galxe. The investors' public statements reveal where the changes occurred. Placeholder's Joel Monegro emphasized performance and the auditability of the exchange, Hashed's Baek Kim valued customer experience, and Wintermute founder Evgeny Gaevoy stressed the team's understanding of crypto trading culture from a market-making perspective. Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko also gave a positive review of Backpack, listing him as a supporter in the announcement, but without specifying whether he personally funded the round. Similarly, Jump's involvement was clearly stated in the 2022 announcement, but the 2024 announcement did not list Jump as a named institution in that round. Kyle Samani disclosed his exposure in more detail. In an article dated September 2, 2026, he wrote that he agreed to join the board before making his personal investment; he then invested $1 million and added another $3 million in the following two months, calling the total $4 million his largest angel investment. Backpack announced his U.S. board appointment on the same day. Samani's logic is that regulated derivatives will return to the U.S., while securities issued on Solana will find use in DeFi. His personal investment is separate from Multicoin's earlier investment in Coral. A shareholding structure chart submitted to the CFTC in July 2026 provides a more precise view of the shareholdings of the exchange's parent company, Trek Labs Ltd: Ferrante holds 36.74%, Linton holds 11.25%, Jump Trading holds 6.07%, and FTX Recovery Trust holds 5.86%. The document assigns 9.85% to Series A investors and 13.77% to employees and others. Can Sun's 16.46% voting rights include its own 6.82% and an irrevocable proxy for Jingjing Sun's 9.64%, meaning the FTX Trust remains a shareholder years after the collapse. This chart is merely a snapshot of the parent company in July and does not disclose the economic terms of the individual Series A securities. In February 2026, Axios reported that the company was in talks to raise $50 million at a pre-money valuation of $1 billion. We were able to verify the negotiations mentioned in the report, but as of November 18, no announcement confirming a closing under those terms had been found. The 2024 consolidated valuation remains the latest pricing and closing we can verify. BP's market capitalization is based on a circulating token price with conditional equity features, used to value Trek Labs or wallet companies, which is a different instrument. What does the US approval cover? On November 13, the CFTC registered TLD Clearing as a Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO). The wording of this order is crucial: TLD can clear margin futures, and its license also covers fully collateralized futures, futures options, and swaps. This distinction determines which instruments can use leverage under this order. On November 16, the CFTC designated TLD Markets as a contract market, authorizing it to operate a trading venue. On November 18, Backpack announced that its affiliated futures commission merchant (FCM) had received NFA approval and become an NFA member. This intermediary is TLC Technologies, operating under the name Backpack Derivatives US. When clients place futures orders, the FCM handles account opening and margin, TLD Markets handles matching, and TLD Clearing acts as the counterparty after clearing. Placing these three functions under the same ownership allows Backpack to directly reach clients while also taking responsibility for the actual operation of each business. Backpack plans to accept eligible fiat and crypto assets as margin, hedge risks between different positions, and provide US traders with 24/7 access to global liquidity. Its own filings describe a phased launch: starting with a limited set of contracts after system testing, clearing member onboarding, and regulatory review. As of November 18, the company was still using the future tense when discussing US trading. The specifications of the initial contracts will be as important as the launch date; they will tell clients what collateral they can submit and which positions can be hedged. The rulebook also explains who bears the losses in the event of a clearing member default. Rule 815 stipulates that the defaulting member's own resources are used first, followed by the clearinghouse's guarantee fund share, and then specific apportionments to surviving members; if these resources are still insufficient, the clearinghouse may terminate the contract in whole or in part. Segregated client margin cannot be used to cover proprietary trading defaults, nor can it be used to cover losses across client account categories. Rule 825 requires public disclosure of the size and composition of funds, as well as contract volume and open interest. These disclosures will allow readers to track the US operations separately from international exchanges.

Where can clients access these products?

In Europe, the two subsidiaries hold different licenses. Trek Labs Europe Ltd (formerly FTX EU Ltd) holds Cyprus Investment Company License 273/15, and its European derivatives platform will launch in September 2025.

What the Trading Data Tells

Perpetual contracts account for approximately 83% of Backpack's daily combined spot and perpetual trading volume. Its perpetual trading volume is equivalent to 1.13% of Hyperliquid's, with an open interest of 0.60% and a perpetual order book depth of 2.78%.

The order book depth metric provides a benchmark for comparing apparent trading volume: Backpack's share of the liquidity in its competitors' quotes is higher than its share of their trading volume, although the absolute difference is still significant. This summary also spans Backpack's 91 perpetual markets and Hyperliquid's 352. A large Bitcoin order at its limit price requires precisely the depth of that contract. Backpack pays for liquidity. Its market maker program invests $325,000 monthly, including $250,000 in perpetual and $75,000 in spot, plus commission rebates. Starting in November, the program's depth multiplier rewards participants who consistently place orders on both sides of the midpoint. The Perps Open from November 12th to 25th also distributed $2,500 daily to traders based on qualified trading volume; the data for November 18th falls within this period. Comparing open interest and market depth after the rewards expire provides a better indication of how much of the demand can be repeated.

How much revenue can these transactions generate? Backpack's entry-level perpetual transaction fee is 2 basis points for limit orders and 5 basis points for takers. VIP rates can be as low as zero for some limit order holders, and market makers also receive rebates. Assuming the venue retains a net 2 basis points for every dollar of reported perpetual trading volume (after deducting fee rebates, excluding separately paid promotional rewards), based on $120.36 million per day and 365 days a year, the fees would be approximately $8.8 million; if it were 1 basis point, it would be approximately $4.4 million. The publicly advertised perpetual reward pool alone would require $3 million to be fully paid out over 12 months. We cannot verify the realized fee revenue, actual incentive expenditures, or group profitability in publicly available financial statements.

More robust data adoption on the stock side

Global tokenized stock spot trading volume, data from Blockworks

Backpack Securities, launched in June, allows eligible clients to hold exposure to the same stock in two ways. By staying with the brokerage, clients hold a security interest through a multi-layered intermediary custody chain; by moving eligible positions to Solana, clients hold transferable tokens representing the underlying asset.

These two forms are easily confused within the application, but the distinction becomes crucial if a customer wants to vote, transfer positions to another brokerage, or redeem purchased tokens on a decentralized exchange. On the brokerage side, accounts are opened by Backpack Securities Global Limited in New Zealand, Atomic Vault Securities is a US-based intermediary brokerage, and RQD Clearing is a clearing brokerage. Backpack states that eligible holdings are eligible for cash dividends. As of November 18th, customer voting functionality remains limited. Eligible whole shares can be transferred in from supported brokerages via free DTC payment, but transfers out from Backpack to other brokerages are not yet available. Therefore, transfers between brokerages and withdrawals to the Solana wallet are two completely different instructions. On the token side, Trek Nexus Markets Ltd or an issuing affiliate acts as trustee. Article 1.18 of the issuance terms stipulates that during the period Backpack Exchange supports these tokens, the issuer recognizes Trek Forge or its designee as the sole beneficiary. Withdrawals give wallet holders control over on-chain transfers, while regular redemption of tokens for brokerage securities still requires a qualifying Backpack account. Direct confirmation under the trust terms is subject to contractual conditions and verification requirements, therefore tokens can change hands on decentralized exchanges even if the new holder is not eligible for redemption through a brokerage. Backpack's tokenized SpaceX stock used Sunrise's issuance infrastructure, one of the earlier listed companies. In November, two new ETFs, SPY and QQQ, and TKO Group Holdings were added. Most brokerage securities trade from 8:00 PM ET Sunday to 8:00 PM ET Friday, with some underlying assets also having weekend order books. When the stocks underlying the tokens are closed on their respective exchanges, the token market continues to trade; therefore, market makers quoting prices on Sundays may continue to bear price risk until the underlying market reopens. Bitwise and Allium analyzed all Solana tokenized stocks and found that regular US trading hours accounted for only 19% of the total trading hours in the quarter, yet contributed 39% of the DEX trading volume in the third quarter, with trading significantly lighter on weekends and holidays. The strongest evidence for product adoption also comes from this third-quarter data. Across all issuers, Solana tokenized stocks traded $6.93 billion on DEXs, with $669 million in outstanding shares at the end of the quarter. Backpack accounts for approximately 44% of trading volume and 4% of outstanding balance, while xStocks' corresponding figures are 50% and 77%, respectively. In terms of value, Backpack's rounded share corresponds to approximately $3.05 billion in quarterly turnover, with approximately $27 million in outstanding balance at the end of the quarter. The latter figure represents the balance at a specific point in time; dividing the two doesn't indicate the typical investor's holding period, but it does show the scale of trading volume attracted by these instruments relative to their outstanding balance. Trading within a third-party liquidity pool benefits the pool's liquidity provider without incurring fees for Backpack Exchange. Kamino provides holders with a reason to continue holding these assets after trading. On November 4th, the partner described a segregated lending market where clients can borrow USDC using tokenized Micron, SK Hynix, SpaceX, or SanDisk as collateral. Allez Labs sets the collateral ratio and liquidation parameters for each asset, and loans may still be liquidated when the underlying stock market is closed. In the same announcement, the partner stated that the cumulative on-chain transaction volume of Backpack's issued shares has exceeded $7 billion, with over 590,000 holders. Outstanding USDC loans secured by one of these shares serve as evidence of the financing purpose, but the number of holders alone cannot determine the prevalence of this use. Who is already serving these customers? Payward agreed to acquire Bitnomial for up to $550 million in cash and stock. This consideration corresponds to an operating business including technology, customers, and years of regulatory work; to convert it into the value of the Backpack license, these assets must first be divested. On Kraken Pro, clients can already trade Bitnomial contracts with funding fees settled every 8 hours, and can compare execution costs between the two after Backpack launches. ICE is betting on two different fronts simultaneously. An agreement reached on October 29 with Trade[XYZ] plans to establish a new regulated derivatives market on Hyperliquid, with ICE acting as the exclusive operator of the Trade[XYZ] regulated market (pending approval). On the securities front, the independent OKXICE joint venture announced that starting November 23, it will offer 24/7 trading in over 70 digital securities to eligible U.S. clients, a planned launch at the time of research closing. One move is vying for derivatives orders, the other for stockbroker clients. ICE expects brokers and platforms, including its joint venture with OKX, to distribute the proposed derivatives contracts. What to Look For in the First Batch of US Trading Data These November approvals have changed what investors can finally measure. The most compelling evidence today comes from traders buying and selling Backpack shares on Solana, while the least transparent figure is how much Backpack actually earns from this use. On international exchanges, publicly available fees and published reward budgets explain why cumulative trading volume doesn't answer the profitability question. The number of active accounts with funds, repeat borrowing, and revenue after deducting rebates are what make existing businesses easier to value. For US futures, the first meaningful comparison will be contract-by-contract: How much BTC or ETH can be executed in a single order near the quoted price? How much open interest remains at the end of the month after the referral rewards expire? Clearinghouse rulebooks require disclosure of trading volume and open interest by contract, and the CFTC will also publish some of FCM's financial data monthly. Reported positions and client funds will be a better indicator of adoption than trading volume records from the first day of launch. Backpack has already secured the right to compete for these balances; whether traders will leave their balances there is another half of the story that begins after launch.
